metaTitle: Brown Banded Cockroach: Light-Colored Roach ID
metaDescription: Brown banded cockroaches are small roaches with two pale bands across the body, hiding high in furniture and electronics. Photos, vs German, look-alikes.
h1: Brown-Banded Cockroaches: The Light-Colored Roach in Furniture and Electronics
dek: Real photos of the small roach with two pale bands across its body, how to tell it from a German cockroach and other light-colored roaches, where it hides, and what its egg cases and droppings look like.
excerpt: Photos and a quick-ID table for the brown-banded cockroach, the small light-colored roach with pale bands: vs German, look-alikes, hiding places and egg cases.

quickAnswer.lead: **A brown-banded cockroach is a small roach, about 1/2 to 5/8 inch long, with two pale bands running across its wings and body instead of the two dark stripes a German cockroach has behind its head.** Males are golden tan and females darker brown, according to [UC IPM's cockroach guide](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/cockroaches/), and both favor warm spots in furniture and electronics.
bullets: [Penn State Extension's fact sheet](https://extension.psu.edu/brown-banded-cockroaches) gives males as about 1/2 inch long and [Texas A&M's](https://urbanentomology.tamu.edu/cockroaches/brown-banded-cockroach/) gives adults as 1/2 to 5/8 inch, about the size of a German cockroach.

Behind the head it has a black bell-shaped mark instead of the German cockroach's two dark lengthwise stripes, says the [University of Kentucky's cockroach fact sheet](https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef614).

A male's light brown wings cover his narrow body and can hide the bands, [Clemson University](https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/cockroach-control/) notes, while the broader female's wings stop short of the tip of her abdomen.
UC IPM says it prefers about 80°F, 5 to 10°F warmer than the German cockroach, and Penn State finds it nearer the ceiling than the floor and away from water.
Females glue light brown egg cases about 1/4 inch long to ceilings, under furniture and in closets, sometimes many together, according to UC IPM.
Kentucky calls it far less common than the German cockroach, and UC IPM puts it at about 1% of indoor infestations in California.

body.text: What does a brown-banded cockroach look like?

A brown-banded cockroach (*Supella longipalpa*) is a small roach marked by two pale bands across its wings and body. The [University of California's Pest Notes on cockroaches](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/cockroaches/) (UC IPM) give adults as about 1/2 inch, with light-colored bands on the abdomen, the wings and the sides of the shield behind the head; [Texas A&M's Urban and Structural Entomology Program](https://urbanentomology.tamu.edu/cockroaches/brown-banded-cockroach/) gives 1/2 to 5/8 inch and calls the bands yellow.

body.alt: Male and female brown-banded cockroaches side by side from above on a pale background: a slim, golden-tan male whose wings cover his body and a broader, darker female with shorter wings
body.caption: A male (left) and a female (right) brown-banded cockroach, labeled on this CDC photo. The male's wings cover his whole abdomen; the broader, darker female's wings stop short of the tip.
body.credit: CDC (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: The shield behind the head is the quickest check. The [University of Kentucky's cockroach fact sheet](https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef614) says the brown-banded cockroach has a black bell-shaped mark there instead of the German cockroach's dark lengthwise stripes. Despite the name, the bands are paler than the body: the [University of Florida's cockroach photo guide](https://entnemdept.ufl.edu/projex/gallery/dl/cockroaches/text/brownbanded_cockroach.htm) calls them pale brown.

body.needed: An adult brown-banded cockroach photographed in a home (on a ceiling, inside a cabinet or on an appliance) beside a coin or a ruler marked in inches, identified by an entomologist or extension service; public domain or CC0 so it can lead the page

body.text: How can you tell a male from a female?

By shape, color and wings. UC IPM describes males as golden tan and females as darker brown, and [Penn State Extension's fact sheet](https://extension.psu.edu/brown-banded-cockroaches) says females are shorter and stouter, with wings that do not cover the whole abdomen. Walter Ebeling's *Urban Entomology* (1975), hosted by [UC Riverside's entomology department](https://entomology.ucr.edu/ebelingchapter6), gives males as 13 to 14.5 mm long (about 1/2 to 9/16 inch) and females as 11 to 12 mm (about 7/16 to 1/2 inch).

On a male the bands can be hard to see, because his light brown wings completely cover his narrow body, [Clemson University's cockroach fact sheet](https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/cockroach-control/) explains; Ebeling places them at the base of the wings and about a third of the way down. Only males fly: UC IPM says they sometimes fly when disturbed, especially above 85°F, and that females cannot. [The guide to flying cockroaches](/blog/can-cockroaches-fly) compares the other species.

body.alt: Tan brown-banded cockroach head down on a white painted wall just under a ledge, with spiny pale legs and a pale band across its wings behind the dark shield over its head
body.caption: An adult brown-banded cockroach on a white wall just under a ledge in Austin, Texas. Note the pale band across the wings just behind the dark shield over the head.
body.credit: (c) Alec Gosewehr, some rights reserved (CC BY-SA), via iNaturalist

body.text: How do you recognize brown-banded nymphs?

They are wingless, with the same two bands, even bolder. Texas A&M says the yellow bands across the back are more pronounced on nymphs than on adults, Penn State places them at the base of the abdomen and at mid-abdomen, and Clemson says all stages carry them. [What baby cockroaches look like](/blog/what-do-baby-cockroaches-look-like) compares the young of every common species.

body.alt: Young brown-banded cockroach held between two fingertips, with a dark head shield and pale yellowish bands across its body
body.caption: A brown-banded cockroach nymph held between two fingertips, which shows how small the young are. Note the pale bands across the body.
body.credit: (c) Emmett Collins-Sussman, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist

body.text: Brown-banded cockroach vs German cockroach: how do you tell them apart?

Look behind the head and across the back. A German cockroach has two dark stripes running lengthwise behind its head and no bands; a brown-banded has bands and no stripes. They are the same size, which is why the University of Florida says the brown-banded is often mistaken for a German cockroach. [Texas A&M AgriLife Extension's guide to cockroach biology and management](https://extensionentomology.tamu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2017/12/Cockroach-Biol-and-Mngmt_ENTO-037_2017.pdf) describes German adults as light brown and 1/2 to 5/8 inch long, with wings that reach the end of the abdomen, though they do not fly.

body.text: Where you found it is a clue, not a test. Kentucky says brown-banded cockroaches are often found in rooms other than kitchens and bathrooms, and UC IPM says they prefer about 80°F, 5 to 10°F warmer than German cockroaches. But Ebeling reported in 1975 that both species had become most abundant in kitchens and that the two are sometimes found together. The markings settle it.

Telling them apart matters for control. Kentucky says the brown-banded cockroach has markedly different hiding places and habits, Penn State says control strategies for other cockroaches will not be effective against it, and UC IPM calls it especially difficult to control with baits. See [the German cockroach guide](/blog/german-cockroaches) for the kitchen species and [the complete guide to cockroaches in US homes](/learn/cockroaches) for the rest.

body.needed: A brown-banded cockroach and a German cockroach side by side at one scale, seen from above beside a ruler marked in inches, showing the bell-shaped mark and pale bands against the two dark stripes; identified by an entomologist or extension service; public domain or CC0

body.text: Is a light-colored cockroach a brown-banded cockroach?

Sometimes. A small, light brown or tan roach indoors is usually a German cockroach, which Kentucky calls far more common, or a male brown-banded cockroach; the stripes or bands tell you which. Texas A&M notes that cockroaches can be brown, black, tan, reddish orange or pale green, so color alone settles little. The table at the top of this page lists the light-colored roaches most likely in or around a US home.
A white or cream roach: it has just molted

UC IPM says cockroaches are white immediately after molting and darken as the new outer covering hardens, usually within hours, so a pale roach that darkens in a closed jar is an ordinary one of its species. [The guide to white cockroaches](/blog/white-cockroach) explains what a white roach means.
A German look-alike at the porch light: the Asian cockroach

The [University of Florida's guide to cockroaches and their management](https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IG082) says the Asian cockroach looks very much like a German cockroach, except that it flies. It lives outdoors, flies to porch lights and finds its way inside, but survives poorly there; UF lists it among the cockroaches most common in and around Florida homes, and Texas A&M says it may be found outdoors in parts of Texas. [Which cockroaches can fly](/blog/can-cockroaches-fly) sorts the fliers.

body.needed: An adult Asian cockroach (Blattella asahinai) identified by an entomologist or extension service, ideally at a porch light or on a lit wall at night; any license on record works for a look-alike card

body.text: Tan roaches from outdoors: Turkestan and wood cockroaches

In California and Texas, a yellowish roach outdoors may be a male Turkestan cockroach: brownish yellow and 1/2 to 7/8 inch long, with pale edges on the shield behind the head and the upper corners of the front wings, says Texas A&M, which calls it one of the most common outdoor roaches in El Paso. UC IPM finds it in water meter boxes, compost, leaf litter and potted plants. The dark, short-winged female resembles [an Oriental cockroach](/blog/oriental-cockroaches).

Near woods, a light brown roach that flew to a light at night may be a male wood cockroach. [Penn State Extension's wood cockroach fact sheet](https://extension.psu.edu/wood-cockroaches) describes males up to 1 inch long, light brown to nearly black, some with cream-edged wings, that are sometimes drawn to lights in rural areas, come in by accident and die indoors within a few days. [Bugs that look like cockroaches](/blog/bugs-that-look-like-cockroaches) covers them.
A big reddish-brown roach: the American cockroach

A roach longer than about an inch is not a brown-banded cockroach. Texas A&M describes the American cockroach as reddish brown and 1 1/2 to 2 inches long, with tan to light-yellow bands outlining the shield behind the head; both sexes can fly. It goes by another name in [the palmetto bug guide](/blog/palmetto-bugs).

body.text: Where do brown-banded cockroaches hide?

In warm, dry, dim places, often high and away from water, in any room. Penn State finds them nearer the ceiling than the floor, Texas A&M says they appear to need less water than other cockroaches, and Kentucky says they are often in rooms other than kitchens and bathrooms. Check:

items: **Walls and ceilings.** Ceilings of dark or dimly lit rooms, behind picture frames and in light switches (Texas A&M), doorframes (Penn State) and wall decorations (UC IPM).
**Cabinets and closets.** The upper walls of cabinets and closets (Texas A&M), pantries (Penn State) and corners near the ceiling (Clemson).
**Furniture.** Beneath or inside furniture (Kentucky), inside upholstered pieces (Texas A&M), dressers, tables and chairs (Penn State) and hollow furniture legs (UC IPM).
**Electronics and appliances.** Crevices in or near electrical appliances (UC IPM), refrigerator motor housings, clocks and radios (Penn State), and, in Ebeling's 1975 account, television sets.
**Clutter.** UC IPM lists accumulations of clutter among their favored hiding places.

body.alt: Young brown-banded cockroach on a textured wall, dark brown with one pale band just behind its head shield and another across the middle of its body, with long thin antennae
body.caption: A brown-banded cockroach nymph on a textured wall. Both pale bands show clearly: one just behind the shield over the head and one across the middle of the body.

body.text: Kentucky calls the species far less common than the German cockroach, and UC IPM, writing for California, puts it at only about 1% of indoor infestations there. Texas A&M finds it more often in homes, apartments, hotels, nursing homes and hospitals than in restaurants and grocery stores. Originally African, it occurs throughout the US, says the University of Florida; Ebeling dates the first US record to Key West and Miami in 1903.
Where do brown-banded cockroaches glue their egg cases?

On hidden surfaces, often above the floor and sometimes many together. UC IPM says females glue the light brown cases, about 1/4 inch long, to ceilings, beneath furniture or in dark places such as closets; Kentucky calls them pea-sized and finds them under dressers and tables; Clemson adds drawers and the inside of furniture and appliances, including TVs, microwaves, computers and radios.

body.alt: Four small, reddish-brown, ridged cockroach egg capsules stuck to a pale wooden surface, seen close up, with a few dark specks nearby
body.caption: Four brown-banded cockroach egg capsules on what appears to be a wooden surface, in a CDC photograph. This is a close-up: UC IPM puts each case at about 1/4 inch long.
body.credit: CDC (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: Penn State says a female carries each capsule for about 30 hours before fastening it in a hidden spot (Ebeling gives 24 to 36 hours) and makes about 14 in her adult life, each holding an average of 13 eggs. [What cockroach eggs look like](/blog/cockroach-eggs) compares the cases of every common species.

body.needed: A female brown-banded cockroach carrying her egg case, or a cluster of egg cases glued under a drawer or inside an appliance, beside a ruler marked in inches, identified by an entomologist or extension service; public domain or CC0

body.text: What are the signs of brown-banded cockroaches?

Tiny droppings, glued egg cases, and roaches or feeding damage away from the kitchen. CDC's 1964 [pictorial key to droppings](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/13428) gives average dry brown-banded droppings as about 1/32 inch, oval, pointed and ridged, half the length of German cockroach droppings and the smallest in the key; it advises judging groups, not single droppings. [What roach poop looks like](/blog/cockroach-droppings) shows each species' droppings.

Their food leaves marks too. UC IPM says they prefer starchy foods such as the glue on stamps and envelopes, and Penn State lists feeding signs on stamps, envelopes, older book bindings, draperies and occasionally wallpaper. [The guide to signs of cockroaches](/blog/signs-of-cockroaches) covers shed skins, smears and the musty smell.

Sticky traps show where they are. Penn State advises traps against a wall or in a corner of a floor, shelf or drawer, at ten or more sites for a week; with this species, include upper cabinets. A separate guide explains [how sticky traps and bait stations do different jobs](/blog/best-roach-traps-canada).
How do brown-banded cockroaches spread to new homes?

By being carried, often as egg cases glued to furniture and appliances, a habit Ebeling says spreads the species over great distances. UC IPM advises checking appliances, furniture, boxes and things recently in storage for egg cases as they come into a building, and removing any you find. Penn State notes that cockroaches also arrive in boxes, grocery bags and suitcases, and Texas A&M says that once established, they can move from one apartment to the next.

Warmth helps decide whether they stay: Ebeling wrote in 1975 that brown-banded infestations generally occur only in homes kept warmer than most people find comfortable. [Where cockroaches come from](/blog/where-do-cockroaches-come-from) covers every route in and how to close it.
Are brown-banded cockroaches dangerous?

They can carry germs onto food and trigger allergies and asthma, like other indoor cockroaches. The [EPA's guide to asthma triggers](https://www.epa.gov/asthma/asthma-triggers-gain-control) says cockroach droppings or body parts can trigger asthma and that proteins in their feces and saliva can cause allergic reactions or asthma symptoms in some people. Kentucky adds that many people are allergic to cockroach excrement and shed skins.

UC IPM reports that indoor cockroaches have been identified as risk factors for asthma developing in children, with allergen levels tracking cockroach numbers. Penn State says bacteria and protozoa that cause diseases such as gastroenteritis and diarrhea can be carried on cockroaches' legs and bodies and deposited on food and utensils.

body.title: Asthma or allergies at home?
body.text: The EPA advises people with asthma to work with a doctor to identify their triggers and develop a treatment plan, so mention the cockroaches if anyone at home has symptoms. It also suggests airtight food containers, prompt cleanup of crumbs and spills, and sealing cracks around cabinets.
How do you get rid of brown-banded cockroaches?

Identify them first and treat where they actually live, because the usual kitchen approach falls short: UC IPM says brown-banded cockroaches are especially difficult to control with baits, and Penn State says residual sprays and aerosol foggers are of little value against them and may disperse them. In order:

items: **Confirm the species.** Check for bands or stripes, and trap at ten or more spots for a week, shelves and drawers included.
**Search high and inside things.** Upper cabinets and closets, behind pictures, under and inside furniture, and around electronics and appliance motors.
**Remove egg cases** glued under furniture, in appliance motors or in boxes, as UC IPM advises, and check what you bring in.

**Follow a full plan.** [The step-by-step plan for getting rid of cockroaches](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-cockroaches) covers bait placement for this species, cleanup and sealing, with [a Canadian edition](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-cockroaches-canada) for readers in Canada.

body.title: Not sure what you caught?
body.text: Photograph it beside a ruler marked in inches, or keep it in a sealed jar, and note where you found it and whether it has bands or stripes. Penn State suggests your county extension office for help, and [the five-question pest identifier](/tools/what-bug-is-this) tells a cockroach from other household pests.

faqs.question: Why do I have brown-banded roaches in my house?
faqs.answer: Often because they or their egg cases came in on something. Walter Ebeling's Urban Entomology says females glue their egg cases to furniture and other household objects, which spreads the species over great distances, and UC IPM advises checking appliances, furniture, boxes and stored items for egg cases as they come into a building. Warmth helps them settle in: UC IPM says the species prefers about 80°F, and Ebeling found infestations generally only in homes kept warmer than most people find comfortable.

faqs.question: Are brown-banded roaches as bad as German roaches?
faqs.answer: They are less common and slower to multiply, but they hide all over the home and can be hard to bait. The University of Kentucky calls them far less common than German cockroaches, and UC IPM puts a brown-banded female and her offspring at over 600 cockroaches a year, against over 30,000 for a German female. UC IPM also says brown-banded cockroaches are especially difficult to control with baits, and Penn State says strategies that work on other cockroaches will not be effective against them. The EPA's warnings about cockroach allergens and asthma apply to both.

faqs.question: How hard is it to get rid of brown-banded cockroaches?
faqs.answer: UC IPM and Penn State both warn that it can be hard to control. UC IPM says brown-banded cockroaches are especially difficult to control with baits, and Penn State says residual sprays and aerosol foggers are of little value and may disperse them, making control difficult and lengthy, though it calls baiting effective where they hide. Kentucky and Penn State stress identifying the species first, because its hiding places differ from the German cockroach's: upper cabinets, closets, furniture and electronics rather than kitchen cracks alone.

faqs.question: Can brown-banded cockroaches fly?
faqs.answer: Only the males. UC IPM says adult males sometimes fly when disturbed, especially at temperatures above 85°F, and that females cannot fly. Penn State says adult males fly readily when disturbed, and Clemson says males can fly in a warm environment. The female's wings stop short of the tip of her abdomen. A small tan roach that flies to a porch light from outdoors may be an Asian cockroach, which the University of Florida says looks very much like a German cockroach but flies.

faqs.question: How long do brown-banded cockroaches live?
faqs.answer: Adults live for months. In a 1940 laboratory study reported in Walter Ebeling's Urban Entomology, adults lived 131 to 315 days, 206 on average, and Penn State gives the adult female's life span as 13 to 45 weeks. Reaching adulthood takes a while too: Penn State puts the egg stage at 37 to 103 days, depending on temperature, and the nymph stage at 8 to 31 weeks, and the University of Florida gives about 160 days on average from egg to adult.

faqs.question: What are brown-banded roaches attracted to?
faqs.answer: Warmth and dry, out-of-the-way places. UC IPM says the species prefers about 80°F, 5 to 10°F warmer than the German cockroach, and Texas A&M says it appears to need less water than other cockroaches and occupies drier locations in a building. Penn State finds it nearer the ceiling than the floor and away from water, in spots such as upper cabinet walls, closets, dressers and the space behind picture frames. For food, UC IPM says it prefers starchy foods.

faqs.question: Does one brown-banded cockroach mean an infestation?
faqs.answer: One is a reason to check rather than proof. It may have arrived on furniture, a box or an appliance, but UC IPM says this species lives and breeds entirely indoors, so look for more. Set sticky traps against walls and in corners of floors, shelves and drawers at ten or more spots for a week, as Penn State advises, and look for egg cases glued under furniture and drawers and for tiny droppings in upper cabinets and closets.

faqs.question: What kind of roach is tan in color?
faqs.answer: Several small roaches are tan. Clemson describes the German cockroach as pale brown or tan with two parallel black streaks behind the head, and UC IPM describes male brown-banded cockroaches as golden tan, with light-colored bands on the wings and body. Outdoors, the Asian cockroach looks very much like a German cockroach but flies to lights, according to the University of Florida, and Texas A&M describes male Turkestan cockroaches as brownish yellow. Any cockroach is white for a few hours after it molts.

faqs.question: What do brown-banded cockroaches eat?
faqs.answer: They prefer starchy foods. UC IPM names the glue on stamps and envelopes, and Penn State says they feed on a wide variety of materials, including glue or paste, starch and certain dyes, leaving signs of feeding on stamps, envelopes, older book bindings, draperies and occasionally wallpaper. Penn State adds that they have been known to chew nylon stockings, presumably for body oils and skin flakes. Texas A&M says they appear to need less water than other cockroaches.

faqs.question: Do brown-banded cockroaches live in electronics?
faqs.answer: They often hide in and around them. UC IPM lists crevices in or near electrical appliances among their favored hiding places, Penn State names refrigerator motor housings, clocks and radios, and Clemson says their egg cases are often glued in furniture and appliances, including TVs, microwaves, computers and radios. UC IPM also says the species prefers warm places, about 80°F, and advises checking appliances brought into a building for egg cases, including inside their motors.
